name: ONOS (Open Network Operating System)
what_it_is: ONOS is an open-source SDN controller platform that supports the transition from legacy brown-field networks to SDN green-field networks, providing high availability through clustering, distributed state management, and a pluggable southbound architecture. It exposes northbound abstractions including a global network view, network graph, and application intents, and supports both proactive and reactive flow setup modes.
components: Clustering and distributed state management engine
Northbound intent framework (global network view, network graph, application intents)
Graphical UI with multi-layer topology viewing
SDN-IP application (BGP interworking with legacy IP networks)
Bazel-based build system (minimum Bazel 1.0.0, Python 3 required)
measurement: No built-in telemetry or streaming metrics pipeline documented in README
gNMI southbound support enables device-level telemetry subscription
REST API can be polled for topology and flow state
configuration: Network configuration pushed via REST API (JSON-based network config subsystem)
CLI for runtime configuration and debugging
Bazel build configuration for component inclusion
Environment variables and JVM flags for cluster node discovery
fault_injection: No built-in fault injection framework documented
Cluster node removal/isolation can be simulated manually via network partitioning
modes: Reactive flow setup (on-demand rule installation triggered by packet-in events)
constraints: Requires Bazel minimum version 1.0.0 and Python 3 for building from source
High-availability clustering requires manual cluster formation and node address configuration
No documented built-in fault injection or chaos testing support
Southbound protocol support is driver-dependent — not all protocols available for all device types
notable_absences: No docker-compose.yml found at repository root (404 on master branch)
No built-in network traffic measurement or telemetry aggregation pipeline
No documented security or authentication configuration beyond basic UI credentials
No built-in fault injection or chaos engineering tooling
No documented performance benchmarks or scalability limits in README
